title: Shurpanakha
hook: the joking stops when she lunges at Sita, and what follows will start a war

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shurpanakha, part one. Ravana's sister demanded Rama marry her, and the brothers answered with jokes. Did you check whether a joke would land kindly? Day five hundred sixty-two.

Shurpanakha has been sent back and forth between the brothers, laughed at, and refused. Now she turns on the person she blames. It's because of her, she says, looking at Sita. I'll eat her right now, and then you'll be mine. And she rushes at Sita. Valmiki compares it to a great meteor hurtling toward a gentle star. Sita, who has said nothing through any of this, is terrified. There's no more time for jokes.
screen: `SHE BLAMES SITA.` → `A METEOR AT A GENTLE STAR.` → `NO MORE JOKES.`

segments.voice: Rama catches her, holds her back, and speaks sharply to Lakshmana. We shouldn't joke with the cruel, he says. Look how close Sita came. Mark her, so she can't do this again. And Lakshmana draws his sword and cuts off her nose and ears. Shurpanakha flees screaming into the forest, bleeding, to her brother Khara at Janasthana. It's a violent scene, and a hard one to sit with. How have people read it? Some devotional readers see it simply: a rakshasi tried to kill Sita, and the brothers stopped her without taking her life. Others, especially modern readers, have found the punishment harsh, all the more after the teasing that came before. Different tellings handle it differently. In some later versions, like Kamban's Tamil Ramayana and Tulsidas's Hindi Ramcharitmanas, she first appears in a beautiful disguise, which changes how the scene feels. And in recent decades, writers have retold the story from Shurpanakha's own side: rejected, mocked, wounded. There's no single reading everyone shares, and it's fine to hold the discomfort. What the text makes plain is that this is a hinge in the story. Her wound goes first to Khara, and from Khara, the story will travel to Lanka, to Ravana. A rejected proposal at a hut by a river leads, step by step, to Sita's abduction and a war. Valmiki lets you watch it happen: a disaster that starts small, with hurt and pride on more than one side.
screen: `MARK HER SO SHE CAN'T DO THIS AGAIN.` · `SHE FLEES TO KHARA.` · `READERS DIFFER.` · `TOLD FROM HER SIDE.` · then, large: `THE HINGE OF THE STORY.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe slowly. Think of a conflict you've seen grow from something small: a family quarrel, a falling out at work, a feud online. Picture its first moment, before it became big. Notice how many people's hurt and pride got involved along the way. You don't have to fix anything. Just breathe with the knowledge that small moments matter, and let your breath stay calm and even. The bell holds the time.
Shurpanakha. She attacks Sita, Lakshmana cuts off her nose and ears, and she flees to Khara. The road to war begins here.
Your line: Shurpanakha. Today, notice one small moment of hurt or pride before it grows, yours or someone else's. Day five hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: The mutilation of Shurpanakha is staged in Ramlila performances, and it is much discussed in modern Ramayana retellings and criticism.

original.note: Sanskrit janasthāna: the region of Dandaka ruled by Khara, where Shurpanakha runs.

trapdoor: what you thought: Shurpanakha's story is a short, simple fight.
what it means: her wounding sets off everything that follows, up to the war.
what a scholar hears: Aranya 18 has Lakshmana disfigure her on Rama's word; later tellings recast the scene, and modern ones tell it from her side.

Reviewer: 'a demon' changed to 'a rakshasi', and 'others, ancient and modern' softened to 'especially modern readers', since pre-modern criticism of the punishment was not sourced. A Keeper may know older commentators who raised it.
Reviewer: 'mark her' is a soft rendering of Rama's instruction (Valmiki's sense is closer to 'disfigure her'); a Keeper should decide whether the softer word hides too much.

Editor review: softened 'many devotional readers', 'nobody disputes' and 'the hinge of the Ramayana' to what the text supports, removed the superlative 'one of the most discussed scenes' in howItsDone, fixed a doubled 'especially', and replaced the generalization about 'great disasters' and pride 'on every side'.
